title: CLEAR: Calibrated Learning for Epistemic and Aleatoric Risk
claim: Separately estimated noise and data-limitation uncertainties each miss something; a calibrated combination yields intervals that adapt to both.
layout: 2 side-by-side scatter panels, left-to-right, overlaid shaded interval bands with legends
description: Two side-by-side scatter plots with X and Y axes. The left panel shows a nonlinear regression curve in purple through dense dark data points concentrated near X=0. A blue band, labeled aleatoric uncertainty, is wide where data are dense and noisy. An orange band, labeled epistemic uncertainty, is narrow within the data region and flares out at the extremes where data are sparse. The right panel uses the same setup with three overlaid interval bands: CLEAR (green outline), CQR (blue) and Ensembles (PCS) (orange). The CLEAR band is tighter than the orange band in the sparse tails. It is wider than the blue band outside the data region and close to it inside. The legend sits at the upper left of each panel, and the eye goes first to the overlapping colored bands.
caption: Left: Blue represents aleatoric uncertainty, which reflects randomness inherent in the data such as measurement noise. Red represents epistemic uncertainty, which arises from limited sample size. Right: Estimated prediction sets using the CLEAR method, which combines both sources of uncertainty in a data-driven manner.
abstract: Accurate uncertainty quantification is critical for reliable predictive modeling. Existing methods typically address either aleatoric uncertainty due to measurement noise or epistemic uncertainty resulting from limited data, but not both in a balanced manner. We propose CLEAR, a calibration method with two distinct parameters, $Î³_1$ and $Î³_2$, to combine the two uncertainty components and improve the conditional coverage of predictive intervals for regression tasks. CLEAR is compatible with any pair of aleatoric and epistemic estimators; we show how it can be used with (i) quantile regression for aleatoric uncertainty and (ii) ensembles drawn from the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework for epistemic uncertainty. Across 17 diverse real-world datasets, CLEAR achieves an average improvement of 28.3\% and 17.5\% in the interval width compared to the two individually calibrated baselines while maintaining nominal coverage. Similar improvements are observed when applying CLEAR to Deep Ensembles (epistemic) and Simultaneous Quantile Regression (aleatoric). The benefits are especially evident in scenarios dominated by high aleatoric or epistemic uncertainty. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/clear/
